newsitem.title: CANADA: Ag Canada sees record 1996/97 grain/oilseed output.
newsitem.headline: Ag Canada sees record 1996/97 grain/oilseed output.

text.p: Agriculture Canada said Tuesday grain and oilseed production in crop year 1996/97 (Aug/July) may reach a record 65 million tonnes.
That output would be nine percent above the 1995/96 level of production and 14 percent above the 10-year average.

Agriculture Canada based its forecast on a July 26 to Aug 2 Statistics Canada survey of farmers but lowered the yield slightly from StatsCan's estimate to reflect the effect of weather, pests and disease since the survey was done.
Wheat and coarse grain prices were expected to remain strong but slightly lower than 1995/96.
Oilseed prices were expected to increase.
Total Canadian production of all grains and all oilseeds was forecast at 64.74 million tonnes with 30 million tonnes exported.
World wheat prices were expected to remain near current levels until December when the Australian and Argentine wheat harvest begins. Those crops were expected to be above average.
World prices will likely decline after December.
World supply and demand of grains and oilseeds will be tight in 1996/97 and prices were expected to be highly volatile due to low global carry-in stocks, Ag Canada said.
Canadian wheat output in 1996/97 was forecast to rise 19 percent from last year to 24.6 million tonnes. Supplies should rise 17 percent to the highest level since 1993/94.
Exports were forecast to rise 32 percent to 17.2 million tonnes, equal to the 10-year average.
Domestic feed grain use was expected to decline but remain at an historically high level.

Durum production was forecast to slip eight percent from last year to 4.36 million tonnes while supplies should be higher than the previous year due to more carry-in stocks. Exports were expected to decline marginally.

Barley output and supplies were seen up 20 percent and feed use was expected to remain strong due to strong livestock demand and low barley prices. Exports were forecast to increase significantly. Ending stocks should rise 50 percent.

Canola stocks were expected to drop 13 percent despite near record yields and carry-in stocks of over 1.0 million tonnes. Strong export demand and and expanded domestic crush should keep prices relatively strong. Reductions in the size of the U.S. soybean crop and increased Chinese demand will be key factors to watch. Flax output may fall 10 percent, stocks were very low so prices were seen up 10 to 20 percent.
